intro: In Mersin province, an ancient city waits for you: Uzuncaburç, known in antiquity as Olba-Diocaesarea. Its story runs from the 3rd century BC to the 3rd century AD. This was the sacred centre of the priest-kings of Olba, and today it is famous for the standing columns of the Temple of Zeus Olbios.
history: Uzuncaburç began life as a sanctuary, the sacred heart of the Hellenistic kingdom of Olba. Then came the Romans. Under Emperor Vespasian it was turned into a separate Roman city with a new name: Diocaesarea. The colonnaded street, the theatre and the temples you will see all survive from this period.
structure-1: You are now standing before the Temple of Zeus Olbios, the Hellenistic temple dedicated to Zeus Olbios here at Uzuncaburç. Look up at its columns and imagine the priests who once served the god in this sacred place.
structure-2: Now turn to the Tall Tower. This tall Hellenistic tower stands on the city's northern edge, and it is the very tower that gives Uzuncaburç its name.
structure-5: Here is the Temple of Tyche, a small temple dedicated to Tyche, goddess of fortune. Modest in size, perhaps, but who would not have wanted fortune on their side?
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the Colonnaded Street, and be sure to find your way to the Theatre as well.
facts: Did you know? The city's name means 'tall tower', after the high Hellenistic tower on the city's northern edge, a tower depicted on the city's ancient coins. The Temple of Zeus Olbios is among the earliest Corinthian temples in Anatolia, raised not long after the order itself was devised. The city was ruled by the Teucrids, a dynasty of priest-kings: a rare arrangement in which priesthood and rule sat in the same person. And that twenty-two-metre Hellenistic tower, which gives the village its name, still stands today.
outro: This brings our tour of Uzuncaburç / Olba-Diocaesarea to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These columns have stood for centuries; let them keep standing for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
